As of 227 PM EDT Friday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Gusty winds will continue across Lake Champlain through 
2-4 AM on Saturday. Sustained winds may approach 25 knots at times 
between 9 PM and midnight but winds will generally range from 20-23 
knots. A few gusts closer to 30 knots will be possible, especially 
following sunset, as a subsidence inversion helps to push the 
stronger winds aloft closer to the surface. High pressure on 
Saturday will help the pressure gradient relax and let winds 
diminish to about 10 to 12 knots. Waves could be in the 2-4 ft range 
through the remainder of the day with a persistent north wind in the 
20+ knot range winds waves subsiding closer to 1-3 ft Saturday 
morning.

Widespread frost across the Adirondacks and Northeast Kingdom is 
looking increasingly likely as high pressure settles into the region 
tonight. Winds initially will range in the 5-12 mph range this 
evening but should go light by midnight. At the same time, dewpoints 
will continue to fall as dry air advects into the region. With clear 
skies and light winds, we should radiate out nicely with 
temperatures plummeting as winds begin to relax. This will allow for 
much of northern New York and the Northeast Kingdom to drop into the 
lower to mid 30s which should facilitate frost formation. Outside of 
these locations, it'll still be noticeably chilly with lows in the 
upper 30s to lower 40s.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A 1025 mb high pressure system will be anchored overhead 
on Saturday with plenty of sunshine, light winds, and seasonably 
cool temperatures expected across the region. However, Sunday is 
looking like a much gloomier day with widespread rainfall expected 
from mid-morning through the evening. Models have come into better 
agreement with showing rainfall overspreading all over Vermont and 
northern New York on Sunday while the exact rainfall amounts are a 
bit more uncertain. Both the GFS and ECMWF keep the plume of deeper 
moisture further south across the Mid-Atlantic while the NAM tries 
to inject some of the nearly 2 inch PWAT values into Vermont. Given 
the NAM boundary layer moisture bias, it's feasible it's much too 
high on PWATs and the forecast is much closer to the GFS/ECMWF 
solutions. This will bring widespread rain in the range of a third 
of an inch to two-thitsdays of an inch with localized amounts upward 
of an inch. Should the NAM forecast pan out, we could see double 
those amounts. Even with the worst case scenario, rainfall rates and 
amounts should be low enough that no flooding concerns are expected; 
especially given the extended period of drier weather we have seen 
over the past 30-45 days.

High pressure will build back in to begin the week with some gusty 
north winds possible on Monday as the pressure gradient remains 
tight. Winds will weaken throughout the day on Monday as high 
pressure becomes further entrenched which could set the stage for 
some fog Monday night.

KEY MESSAGE 3: A Rex block pattern will develop early to mid next week 
as high pressure over the northern Great Lakes shifts east into 
central Quebec, with troughing developing over the Mid-Atlantic. 
Ridging associated with the high over Canada will nudge into 
northern New England keeping us dry through mid next week with good 
ensemble agreement in cold air damming across eastern Vermont. Clear 
skies and subsidence under the ridge will draw seasonably cool air 
south with highs in the 60s, and overnight lows in the low 30s to 
the low 40s. Under the coolest nights if good radiational cooling 
becomes more apparent, frost will be possible each night Tues-Thu in 
the climo favored areas of the Adirondacks and central/northeastern 
Vermont.

Towards the end of the work week next week, a coastal low off the 
Mid-Atlantic will possibly open as it slowly tracks north towards 
southern New England. Under the Rex Block, moisture from this system 
may nudge slightly north, opening the door for light shower 
potentials late week in our south and eastern zones Thursday and 
Friday.
